questions.question: Which chart is most suitable for comparing values across categories?
options: Bar chart
Pie chart with 20 slices
Scatter plot without axes
Dense 3D cylinder chart

questions.question: What primary mechanism ensures a sample accurately represents a broader population?
options: Probability-based random selection with appropriate stratification
Convenience selection from nearest district offices
Selecting the smallest sample size to minimize errors
Relying solely on voluntary online responses

questions.question: Before reporting a sudden trend shift in official data, what should you verify first?
options: Data collection consistency, methodology changes, and sample quality
The color theme of the presentation slides
The length of the executive summary headline
Whether the trend matches anecdotal opinion

questions.question: What should a high-impact chart title ideally communicate to policy makers?
options: The key takeaway insight or primary conclusion
Only the raw table index and timestamp
A decorative quote unrelated to the data
A generic label like 'Chart 1'

questions.question: Why is rigorous methodology documentation required in official statistics?
options: To guarantee transparency, reproducibility, and international comparability
To make survey documentation unnecessarily long
To obscure underlying statistical assumptions
It is optional when deadlines are tight

Overall Grading........................................... 105 APPENDIX XXXIII Time schedule for preparation/completion of APAR................................... 107 (iii) PREFACE The Lok Sabha Secretariat has consistently endeavoured to evolve as an efficient organization since its inception. The Secretariat has reviewed its systems management, work processes and procedures from time to time and published revised editions of the Manual for the use of its officers and staff. The Manual first published in 1959 as the Manual on Filing Procedure, was revised in 1992 and renamed as the Manual on Office Procedure. This is the fourth revised and enlarged edition of the Manual. The chapters in this volume have been arranged as per the established stages of the filing procedure. It inter alia contains changes that have been introduced in the filing and office procedure after the publication of the third edition in particular, those adjustments necessitated by widespread adoption of the e-office system. Besides, the instructions pertaining to review of performance, observance of punctuality, maintenance of proper office decorum, confidentiality and secrecy of papers, etc., which were brought out in the circulars and instructional orders issued from time to time, have been consolidated and included. Two additional chapters viz. Digital/Social Media and Outreach Content and Cyber Security have been included as new chapters in this edition. Also, Chapter IX of the third edition i.e. Review and Weeding of Records and Chapter VI i.e. Editing and Printing of Important Files Classified under Class 'A' has been suitably merged into Chapter V i.e. Management of Files and Records of this edition. Besides, Chapter X of the third edition i.e. Maintenance of research material, summaries of books, reference material bibliographies, etc. prepared by Committee Branches and LARRDIS has been merged with Chapter VII of third edition constituting a new Chapter VI of this edition i.e. Precedent Register, Entries for various Manuals and Maintenance of Research Material. At the same time, the instructions related to specific procedure pertaining to the functioning of a few individual Branches have been consciously omitted to make the Manual a handbook that contains instructions on procedural matters of general applicability only. I am sure the Manual will serve as an invaluable Guide for the officers and staff of the Secretariat on the systematic handling, submission and maintenance of files and on other such matters. NEW DELHI; UTPAL KUMAR SINGH, January, 2024 Secretary-General. Magha, 1945 (Saka) CHAPTER I DEFINITIONS 1.1 Special meanings to be attached to some of the terms used in the Manual are defined as under:— (1) Appendix to Correspondence —In relation to a file ‘Appendix to Correspondence’ means lengthy enclosures to a communication (whether receipt or issue) on the file, inclusion of which in the correspondence portion is likely to obstruct smooth reading of the correspondence or make the correspondence portion unwieldy. (2) Appendix to Notes—In relation to a file ‘Appendix to Notes’ means a lengthy summary or statement containing detailed information concerning certain aspects of the question(s) discussed on the file, incorporation of which in the main note is likely to obscure the main point or make the main note unnecessarily lengthy. (3) Branch – The fundamental functional component of the Secretariat which may be comprised of Units to execute the task assigned. (4) Branch Officer— A ‘Branch Officer’ is an officer of the level of Deputy Secretary or an officer of equivalent rank, in charge of the Branch(es) and, thereto exercises control on all works related to official mandate/business pertaining to the Branch(es), as well as, maintains discipline amongst the officials under his/her administrative control. (5) Case—A ‘Case’ consists of any piece of official business/request in a file or any ‘Papers under Consideration’ pertaining to the mandate of a Branch or Unit which have to be examined and taken up for approval of the administrative authority with reference to any policy decision or decision for implementation/execution or disposal at the level of a Branch. (6) Central receipt and issue Branch (Distribution Branch)–The Distribution Branch (‘D’ Branch) is the central registry and central issue Branch in the Secretariat. All official Posts - Daks addressed to and or arriving in the Secretariat are received in the ‘D’ Branch and are distributed to the addressee. Similarly, all Posts/Daks originating from various Branches and Units are forwarded to this Branch for in-house and/or outward circulation. (7) Classified Dak —All Posts/Daks bearing Security grading with reference to sensitive inputs/data received in the Secretariat, pertaining to certain issues raised by particular Branch with certain Ministry(ies) or other Department(s) of the Government of India or Organisation may be categorized as ‘Classified’ Posts/Daks. (8) Come-back case —A ‘Come-back’ case means a case received back from its originator for further action, without which it could be considered incomplete or un-disposed for want of re-examination/ review or for preparing a draft or a summary of the topic/subject by the concerned Branch. (9) Correspondence —Correspondence consists of communications received and sent through physical mode (using paper) and ‘e’ mode (email, Whatsapp, SMS, designated portals, etc.) in different forms - letters, Office Memoranda, Demi Official (DO) letters, Notices, etc. from official and non official sources in connection with carrying out of official work’. (Specimens of Letter, Office Memoranda, DO letter and Inter-departmental note placed in Appendix I) (10) Current File —A ‘Current file’ means any such file containing a paper or papers on which action is to be initiated or needs specific action by the concerned Branch of the Secretariat, whereby, it is deemed to be incomplete until its disposal. (11) Dak —A ‘Dak’ is specifically a Post whereby, all types of written communications (such as letter, inter- departmental note, file, fax, e-mail, wireless message) received either through postal services or through Special Messengers or through electronic modes etc., in any Branch/Unit in the Secretariat for consideration of authorities or for appropriate necessary action or as important information. (12) Dealing hand—Any functionary entrusted with initial examination of the case. (13) Demi-Official Correspondence— A Communication is demi-official when Government officers correspond with each other or with any member of the public without the formality of the prescribed 2 procedure and with a view to inter-change or as a means of communication of opinion or information before a formal decision is taken. (14) Divisional Officer—Divisional Officer (i.e. Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) is responsible for the disposal of business dealt with by the Branch(es) under his/her charge and exercises overall supervision in regard to functioning/execution of work, maintaining Office decorum, punctuality, discipline, etc., over the Branches under her/his charge. (15) Docketing—Docketing means making of entries in the note portion of a File about the serial number assigned to each item of correspondence (whether receipt or issue) for its identification. (16) Draft —Draft means a rough copy prepared of a document. The word ‘Drafting’ when used in the Secretariat means composing of official communications, based on officers’ notes or orders. (17) File —File/e-file means a collection of papers on a specific subject-matter, assigned a number (File/e-file No.) and consisting of one or more of — (a) Correspondence; (b) Notes; (c) Appendix to Correspondence; and (d) Appendix to Notes. (18) Filing —Filing can be defined as placing loose matter in some systematic order so that the papers wanted can be located readily. (19) Fresh Receipt—F.R. means any subsequent receipt on a case which brings an additional information to aid the disposal of the paper under consideration. (20) Head of the Branch — An officer of the level of Under Secretary or equivalent rank who executes/ exercises control over the officers/staff posted in the Branch under his/her charge and is responsible for ensuring efficient and expeditious disposal of work in the Branch. In absence of the Under Secretary or equivalent level officer, Executive Officer or equivalent level Officer shall discharge his/her responsibilities. (21) Inter-departmental Correspondence—Any communication through which a paper or a file or a case is forwarded to any other Department(s) for obtaining their concurrence, opinion or remarks on a particular matter for facilitating the competent authority in making decision accordingly. (22) Issue— The term ‘Issue’ or ‘Issuance’ is used to signify the various stages of action after approval of a draft, namely, typing of fair copy, the examination of the typed material, submission of a fair copy for signature and finally the dispatch of the communication to the addressee. (23) Attendant Book—Attendant Book means a record, maintained in form, of particulars of dispatch of non-postal communications and their receipt by the addressees. (24) Notes —A Note means the remark(s) recorded on a case to facilitate its disposal. It includes a precise of previous papers, a statement or an analysis of questions requiring decision, suggestions regarding the course of action and final orders passed thereon. (25) Official Correspondence— An Official Correspondence means any communication addressed by or to any Government Official, Public Body or Private Individual, seeking or providing information in conformity with the prescribed form and procedure. (26) Paper Under Consideration—The Paper Under Consideration (P.U.C.) is normally a primary receipt, the consideration of which is the subject matter of the case to be taken on a File for submission/ disposal. (27) Receipts— Receipt encompasses all/various communications (whether official/demi-official or un- official) received in the Secretariat or by any Officer of the Secretariat in official capacity. (28) Recording—Recording is the process of closing a file after action on all the issues considered thereon has been completed. It includes operations like completing references, removing routine papers, revising the file title, changing the file cover and stitching the file. (29) Referencing—Referencing is the process of putting up and referring to connected records, precedents, rules, regulations, books or any other paper having bearing on the case. (30) Urgent Dak—Urgent Dak means any Dak marked ‘Immediate’ or ‘Priority’, and includes wireless messages, telex messages, fax, e-mails, etc. 3 CHAPTER II COMPOSITION AND MANAGEMENT OF FILE 1. Constituents of a File Main File 2.1 ‘File’ means a folder consisting of related papers on a specific subject consisting of one or more parts with a file number. 2.2 The main parts of a File are (i) ‘Notes’ and (ii) ‘Correspondences’. 2.3 The ‘Note’ contains noting recorded on the ‘Paper under Consideration’ or the request receipt or a ‘Fresh Receipt’, if any, and is to be considered as the process sheet on how decision could be taken in the case by submission for approval of the competent authority. The last paragraph of note contains draft proposal, after due analysis of the case, to be submitted for consideration and approval of the competent authority. 2.4 The ‘Correspondence’ contains all communications received and office copies of out-going communications. It is essentially all incoming written communications that are inputs for taking appropriate decision, and Office copy of the communication sent by the office. 2.5 If the issues depicted in a receipt or in notes or in the orders passed thereon go beyond the original subject, relevant extracts should be taken and dealt with separately in a new file. 2.6 An e-File is a file in electronic form and mainly comprise of: (a) Notes (b) Correspondences (c) Draft communications (d) References (e) Linked files (actionable files) (f) Attached files (linked for reference purposes) Part File 2.7 A part file may be opened when the main file is not likely to be available for some time and it is necessary to process a fresh receipt or a note without waiting for its return, or when the main file has become rather bulky, in which case only the essential papers which are required for the disposal of a point should be submitted with a separate note sheet and not the whole file. 2.8 A part file will normally consist of:– (i) the original ‘ Paper Under Consideration’ or its copy and other essential papers on the ‘Correspondence’ side; and (ii) the note or notes recorded or to be recorded on the ‘Paper Under Consideration’ or a copy thereof on the ‘Notes’ side. 2.9 Part file should be amalgamated with the main file as soon as possible. The duplicate papers, if any, should be removed. 2.10 When more than one part files are opened, each one of them should be given a distinct number, e.g. 5/2/2009/O&M (Part File 1), 5/2/2009/O&M (Part File II). 2.11 The dealing hand concerned should invariably maintain a list of part files opened by him/her. 2.12 In e-File, the part file is opened against a main file by any user if he/she is in the channel of submission of that file. Unlike the merger of physical files, in e-File, part file is attached as separate entity and subsequently the respective part files are closed. However, Physical files can be merged together and closed or can be closed separately depending upon the case. Collection Cover 2.13 It contains routine notes of secondary information, casual correspondence exchanged for collecting further information from various sources, r eminders, acknowledgements, and other KW (Keep With) papers, 4 which are not appropriate to form part of the main file. Only the gist of the material collected in the collection cover is incorporated in the main file. 2.14 Many of the items assembled in the collection cover will be of only temporary value. At the time of recording of file, the papers which have lost their value should be destroyed under the direction of the Branch Officer. 2.15 Collection cover must not leave the Branch to which it belongs. 2. File Register 2.16 Each Branch/Unit will open a file register. General Procurement and General Store Branches will be responsible for printing, stock, issue, etc., of the file registers. The register will be in the form enclosed at Appendix-II & III and neatly bound. It will be a permanent record and therefore, will contain adequate number of sheets according to the needs of each Branch/Unit. 2.17 As soon as a new file is opened, the number and subject allotted to it should be entered in the file Register. A record of files opened during a calendar year/during the yearly term of the Committee will be kept in the file register. Entries for the next year will be made either in a new file register or in the same register where pages will be allocated year-wise. 2.18 The entries in the file register will be made legibly, and erasures, omissions and overwriting will be avoided. All entries will be in blue ink only. 2.19 The file register will be placed in a central place in the Branch/Unit under the custody of Senior Secretariat Assistant/Secretariat Assistant etc. as decided by the Branch/Unit Head for reference but in no case shall it be roughly handled. 3. Opening and numbering of new files 2.20 There should be a separate file for each distinctive subject. If the subject of a file is too wide or too general, there will be a tendency to place in it papers dealing with different aspects of the matter which apart from making the file unwieldy will impede work. 2.21 The system of opening and numbering of new files broadly accepted for general application in the Lok Sabha Secretariat is based on subject classification. The main subjects ordinarily dealt with in a Branch/ Unit are known as ‘Standard Headings’. Some subjects yield to further sub-division i.e. ‘Sub-Headings’. 2.22 To enable the files to be easily traced at a moment’s notice, an alphabetical list of contents, as shown in Appendix-II will be prepared at the beginning of the file register indicating the ‘ Standard Headings’ and ‘Sub-Headings’ and the pages allotted to them. 2.23 The list will be scrutinised and brought up-to-date at the beginning of every calendar year or the term of the Committee. As far as possible the main subjects will be allotted the same standard file number year after year. A new heading may be added to the list with the approval of the Head of the Branch/Unit during the course of the year, if found necessary. 2.24 When it is necessary to open a new file, the dealing hand will first ascertain from the list the ‘Standard Heading’ under which it should be opened. The official concerned will then prepare a suitable title for the new file and allot it a number (next available in the serial order in the file register) under the ‘Standard Heading’. 2.25 The title of the file should indicate the subject matter of the case in as few words as possible. The first words of the title should almost always be the main subject under which the file is being opened and the descriptive part of the title should then follow. Thus, for instance, the subject of a new file opened under the main subject ‘Lok Sabha Secretariat (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules’ will be ‘Lok Sabha Secretariat (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules—Delegation of authority to impose punishment’. The title should be so framed that it would show at a glance the subject-matter dealt with and enable the file to be easily identified. The title of the file should be approved by the Head of the Branch/Unit, before it is actually opened. 2.26 A number given to the file will consist of (i) the number allotted to the ‘ Standard Heading’, (ii) the serial number given to the file under the ‘Standard Heading’, (iii) the year in which opened, and (iv) the initials or letters used for identifying the Branch/Unit. The file will bear the same number and subject as shown in the 5 file register. 2.27 Thus the files opened in O&M Branch during the year 2009 under the Standard Heading ‘Assessment of staff requirements and job analysis by O&M Branch’ will be numbered as follows:— Standard Heading — 2 Main Subject — Assessment of staff requirements and job analysis of Branches by O&M Branch 2/1/2009/O&M — Staff requirements and job analysis of P.N.O. 2/2/2009/O&M — Staff requirements and job analysis of Reporters Branch 2/3/2009/O&M — Staff requirements and job analysis of LARRDIS 2.28 Files may be opened under sub-heads, in case the subject yields to further sub-division. These files will be numbered as under:— Standard Heading — 2 Main Subject — Assessment of staff requirements and job analysis of Branches by O&M Branch. Sub-Heading Staff requirements and job analysis of P.N.O. — 2/1/2009/O&M Sub-Division Consideration of Report on P .N.O. by Administration — 2/1(I)/2009/O&M Implementation of recommendations of O&M by P.N.O./Administration — 2/1(II)/2009/O&M 2.29 A policy file should bear the alphabet ‘(P)’ after the ‘Standard Heading’ number under which the file is opened, in order to distinguish it from other files. Routine action taken or matters dealt with as a result of policy decision should be on a separate file which should be closed at the end of each year. 2.30 Papers will be dealt with and filed in a file without regard to the year to which the references in that file pertain. 2.31 No file should ordinarily contain more that 150 sheets of notes and correspondences. On reaching the maximum limit, a new file should be opened with the same number but marked V ol. II or V ol. III, as the case may be. The previous file should be closed and marked V ol. I. In all subsequent files on the same subject, the previous and later references should be quoted in the space provided for this purpose. If the file relates to the sessional work, it should be closed after each Session irrespective of the fact whether it contains 150 sheets or less. Similarly, a file relating to a Committee will be closed on the expiry of the term of Committee whether it contains 150 sheets or less. 2.32 File numbering in e-File is based on the type of the file numbering system adopted by the Department. In case of functional file system, e-File has a provision to include basic, primary, secondary and tertiary heads in respect of the substantive functions of the Department. e-File also has provision for file numbering system based on subject classification. However, efforts are to be made by each Department to move from the file numbering system based on subject classification to the functional file numbering system. How these are to be done is given in the e-File User manual available at https://docs.eoffice.gov.in/eFileMU.pdf. Closure of e-files 2.33 The files opened in e-office can be closed by submitting those files for closing approval by the user. After attaining approval for closure of the files from the officer concerned, the files can be closed. 4. Management of a file 2.34 When an officer passes an order requiring a file or any matter to be disposed of by a particular date, the individual who is responsible for carrying out that order must comply with it before the date specified. If, however, owing to any circumstances beyond the control of the individual concerned, some delay is inevitable and he/she finds himself/herself unable to finish the work by the date stated in the order, he/she should report accordingly and submit a request for the extension of time together with full reasons which will be considered by the officer who passed the original order. 6 Numbering of pages 2.35 Every page of notes and correspondences should be consequently numbered in separate series with pencil at the top right hand corner from bottom to top. Blank intervening pages, if any, should also be numbered. When there are annexures etc. to the P.U.C., these will bear the number allotted to the P.U.C. followed by alphabet e.g. 15-A, 15-B, 15-C etc. The idea is to distinguish the P.U.C. from an enclosure. Where, however, the enclosures to a communication received or issued consist of a large mass of material, they may be allotted consecutive page numbers, if convenient. Page numbering done in pencil should be inked at the time of recording of the file. Serial Numbers 2.36 Every communication, whether receipt or issue, together with its enclosures kept in the ‘Correspondence’ will be given a serial number in red ink in the centre of its first page. The first communication will be marked ‘Serial No. 1’ and subsequent ones will bear consecutive numbers in a single series. To distinguish ‘Receipt’ and ‘Issue’ communications, the entries should be marked ‘Serial No. 1(R)’ and ‘Serial No. 2(I)’ and so on. 2.37 The serial numbers are useful for the purpose of referring to any paper, as also for ensuring that the file is complete. The loss of a letter is at once detected by the fact that a serial number is missing. The series, therefore, must be carefully kept up. Docketing 2.38 Docketing is the process of making entries in the ‘Notes’ portion of a file about each Serial Number (Receipt or Issue) in the ‘Correspondence’ for its identification. A receipt will be docketed by writing in red ink, across the page, the Serial Number of the communication followed by its number and date and the designation/ name of sender [e.g. Serial No. 4 (Receipt)— No. 2/1/2009-O&M, dated 28 January, 2009 from the Secretary, Bihar Legislative Assembly]. An ‘Issue’ will be docketed by entering the Serial No. given to it, followed by the date of its issue and the name and designation of the addressee [e.g. Serial No. 5 (Issue) dated the 31st January, 2009 to the Secretary, Bihar Legislative Assembly]. Docketing of Part Files 2.39 Docketing in the Part Files should be done in pencil in the following manner:— Serial Number....................................... (Receipt) Serial Number........................................(Issue) 2.40 The pencil entries should be erased when amalgamating the papers with the Main File and the revised entries made in red ink. 2.41 In e-File, the system automatically numbers the e-pages in the Notes and the Correspondences portions in separate series. Thus, page numbers are given automatically by the system. The system facilitates marking a ‘Receipt’ in correspondence as ‘PUC #’ or ‘FR#’. However, once a “PUC” or “FR” number is assigned, it cannot be changed. Therefore, each new “PUC” or “FR” will be assigned a fresh number. In e-File, there is no need to flag correspondence as PUC or FR, as merely giving reference to the page number would suffice to track that reference. 2.42 ‘Docketing’ in e-File is done in two ways: a. There is a provision for the HS/Senior officer to record his/her comments on the ‘Receipt’ in the “Remarks” field. This process is done before adding the ‘Receipt’ in the e-File; and b. It is reproduced by typing the remarks given by the HS or senior officers on the notes portion and hyper-linking the relevant correspondence page number. However, the system does not assign a serial number for docketing, as is done in the manual system. Referencing and use of slips 2.43 Referencing is the process of putting up and referring to connected records, precedents, rules, regulations, books or any other paper having a bearing on a case. Reference to such paper will be made 7 as far as possible by quoting the file number and the page no., in the margin. When absolutely necessary, flags may be used to facilitate the identification of a particular reference. While using slips it should be remembered that the slips are merely a temporary convenience for the quick identification of papers and should be removed as soon as they have served their purpose. To facilitate the identification of references after the removal of slips, it is necessary that the number of the file and the relevant page number referred to should be quoted in the body of the note e.g.:— [F.No. 3/1/AN/2009P-3 Notes] 2.44 Similarly a description of the Rules, Regulations, Act, etc., together with the number of the relevant paragraph or clause referred to, will always be quoted in the body of the note while the alphabetical letters of the slip and the page number will be indicated in the margin. 2.45 Books or Rules etc., referred to need not be put up on a file if copies thereof are available with the officer to whom a case is submitted. This should, however, be indicated in the margin of the notes in pencil. Where it is found necessary to put up books to officers, clean and bound volumes should be put up. 2.46 Whenever any reference is taken from any book, the latest edition of the original book of reference (available in the Parliament Library) should be consulted. Second hand quotations should not be relied upon, but should invariably be checked with the original. The Reference should be authentic and it must be ensured by the dealing hand that the information and source is authentic and correct. 2.47 In e-File, all electronic receipts including scanned copy of PUC and FRs are attached or uploaded to e-File. For electronic Files the need for creating a new volume does not arise. Cross-referencing of correspondence 2.48 In order to know at a glance the latest position in regard to any P.U.C. without going through the whole correspondence, the previous and later references on that P.U.C. will be cross-referenced by marking previous reference and later reference in margin with pencil. In e-File, papers are arranged in each part of the file as given in the paragraph 3.34. There is no need for Appendix to Notes or Appendix to Correspondence in e-File. Linking of files 2.49 When two or more current files on which action is necessary are linked, the printed slip bearing ‘please see also the linked file’ should be pinned to the cover of the topmost file. The number of the linked file should be given on the slip. Linking of files should be avoided as far as possible. Ordinarily, files should be consolidated, whenever practicable, into one file by an intelligent selection and arrangement of papers. Where it is necessary to refer to another file, an extract of the relevant noting, etc. on the file should be made provided it is of reasonable length, and placed on the file for which it is required. Only in those cases where many pages have to be referred to, files should be linked. Heads of Branches should take special care to see that files are linked together only when absolutely necessary are unlinked at the earliest opportunity. If linked files are not received back in the branch within a few days of submission and they are required for the disposal of another reference, the permission of the officer, with whom the files are, should be obtained to unlink them. 2.50 Procedure exists for linking and attaching of files in the e-File. Only active files are available for linking/attaching. The files to be linked or attached must be available in the user’s account. Pinning together of papers 2.51 When the papers in a file are pinned together it should be so done as not to allow the sharp point of the pin to protrude and prick the fingers of any person who handles the file. In order to prevent injuries from pins, the sharp point of the pin should be embedded under the surface of the paper at the top. Punching of papers 2.52 Every paper shall be punched at the left hand top corner to the correct gauge (3/4 of an inch from either side) before it is tagged to the correspondences or notes. 8 Flagging of papers in a file 2.53 A flag bearing the words ‘Paper Under Consideration (P.U.C.) should be attached to the receipt which is being considered. If a receipt has been disposed of and a later receipt is being dealt with on the same file, the P.U.C. slip should be removed from the old receipt and affixed to the new one. If more than one receipt are under consideration at the same time, the P.U.C. slip should be attached to each ‘receipt’ and numbered I, II, III and so on. The receipt should be numbered serially. 2.54 The previous papers put on the file and the recorded proceedings should be flagged with flags bearing different letters. No two flags should be alike in the same file. The flags should be doubled over and pinned neatly to the inside of the cover page. They should not overlap each other when the papers are arranged in the file, but should be distributed along the whole width, so that they may be easily seen. Quick movement of files 2.55 Files disposed of by the Branches during the day must reach the respective Branch Officers the same day preferably at regular intervals. If a file cannot reach the officer concerned on the same day, it must reach him/her the following morning by 10 AM. 2.56 Files passed by higher Officer will be sent directly by Personal Assistant/Private Secretary to the Officer to whom the files are marked after keeping a note of the movement, in his/her diary. 2.57 In case of electronic file or receipt, the movement of the file is recorded in the system automatically, as and when a user sends it to another. However, when a physical receipt or file is sent using e-File, the user has to make sure that the physical receipt or file is actually sent along with a movement entry made in the system. The receiver has to acknowledge the receiving of the receipt or the file in the system as well. Priority marking on files 2.58 The two prescribed priority markings to be used on files and papers are ‘ACTION THIS DAY’ and ‘IMMEDIATE’. 2.59 The label ‘ACTION THIS DAY’ should be used only in cases of extraordinary urgency requiring disposal on a top priority basis like Questions, Notices of Calling Attention, Adjournment Motions, List of Business of the House or ‘subject being examined by a Committee, etc. In all such cases, timings of receipt and disposal should be indicated in the margin of the last note on the file. 2.60 The label ‘IMMEDIATE’ should be used in cases which are assigned a priority lower than the cases referred to in the preceding paragraph but which still require action on the same day. 2.61 The Officers through whom a file passes should examine whether the priority marking, if any, is appropriate, and if not, should remove or change the marking. 2.62 In no case should a file be sent to the residence of an Officer unless so directed by the Officer concerned or under the specific directions of the Branch Officer. 2.63 In e-File, ‘Out Today’, “Most Immediate” and “Immediate” are the urgency gradings. These urgency gradings are given by the user at the time of sending the file/receipt. The grading of urgency assigned to a case will be reviewed by all concerned at different stages of its progress and where necessary, revised. This is particularly important for cases proposed to be referred to other Departments. Parking of e-files 2.64 It contains list of Files that are temporarily closed and work will be done later on. Pendency of File will be removed if any file is parked. Parked files can be made active at any point of time. Details of the procedure to park and close e-files are provided in e-File user manual available at https://docs.eoffice.gov.in/ eFileMU.pdf. Use only neat and clean file covers and file boards 2.65 Only neat and clean file covers and file boards will be used for submitting files. The Heads of Branches will ensure that instructions in this regard are observed strictly by the officers/staff working under them and no torn or dirty file cover or file board is used. 9 CHAPTER III PREPARATION AND SUBMISSION OF CASES Receipts 3.1 All the official Receipts received (in physical form or soft/electronic form through e-Office/e-mail etc.) in the Branch (falling within the mandate or scope of the Branch) must be categorized by the Branch Officer/Head of the Branch in accordance with the nature of action to be taken on them, such as– (i) Receipts of important nature raising new requirements, new questions of policy, modification of existing policy or orders or any other receipts which are not of a routine nature, but requiring immediate attention of the Officers in the Hierarchy; (ii) Receipts of regular or routine nature which have a clear line of action; and (iii) Receipts which are only for information and don’t need any action. Having categorized thus, all these Receipts must be brought to the attention of the dealing hand(s) or Desk for necessary action under his/her supervision or as directed/suggested/advised by the Officers in the channel of submission hierarchy. 3.2 Similarly, all receipts received by the Branch Officer from the hierarchy/authorities must be aptly dealt by himself/herself directly, or if need be, sent to the Head of the Branch for initiating appropriate action by the Branch for information/approval of the competent authority in the matter. 3.3 All Receipts of important/urgent nature must be taken up by the Head of the Branch with the Branch Officer, so that appropriate action is initiated upfront immediately. If any receipt can’t be initiated by the dealing hand on his/her own due to want of proper direction he/she may discuss a clear line of action with the supervising Officer and clear the file for due submission in a professional and ethical manner within the given deadline/time frame. 3.4 All Receipts of primary/routine nature needing clear line of action may be sent to the appropriate dealing hand with precise directions / instruction for submission. 3.5 All Receipts which needs no action of submission by the Branch may be held in abeyance, until they are required to be added to any relevant file, information of which is to be brought to the notice of any competent authority as and when required. Action by the Dealing-hand(s) 3.6 Upon receiving specifically earmarked Receipts (one or more Receipts than one) for action, they must be read and understood and prioritized for initiating appropriate action on each one of these. The Receipts of URGENT ACTION / FOR IMMEDIATE SUBMISSION must be acted upon immediately. Any receipts requiring priority attention must be acted upon subsequently. All Routine Receipts must be attended to within the stipulated timeframe ascribed to them. Bringing a receipt on to a file 3.7 All Receipts will be brought on to a current file if they relate to a subject on which a file already exists. If not, it will be submitted in a fresh / new file. I. What is Noting 3.8 ‘Note’ is remarks recorded on a receipt/paper under consideration to facilitate its disposal. It includes precise of previous papers, analysis of issues requiring decision, financial encumbrances, legal or other implications, if any; along with justified suggestions/recommendations for final decision of the competent authority. ‘Noting’ is the basic process of recording a note on the ‘Notes portion’ of a file. Note is recorded by the ‘dealing-hand/officer’ and the officers in the hierarchy to facilitate decision making by the ‘competent authority’. 10 The objectives of Office Noting 3.9 The objective of Office Noting is to draw attention to previous decisions/precedents/correspondence or rules and orders having a bearing on the subject, and to state the facts on the current issue in a clear and concise manner, highlighting points which require orders, along with appropriate course of action for culmination of the receipt under submission. Prerequisites of Office Noting 3.10 (i) All notes are to be recorded on Note Sheet in Physical file (Green Sheet), and in the Note portion in the e-file. (ii) Note (s) is/are submitted either seeking approval of the competent authority in the matter, or simply for information. (iii) Any Note must be ‘To the point’ and ‘brief’ until otherwise the receipt requires elaboration in detail. Only requisite summary of the issues raised in receipt must be presented in the note. All other information documents such as ‘Verbatim reproduction’ of extracts, fresh receipt, or any other part of correspondence or notes must be placed on the opposite of the Note on the same file (physical) or in the local reference, or linked in the Link Tab in an e-file. (iv) For efficient noting and to decide the quantum of noting for successful submission, guidelines given on functional approach to noting are to be adopted. (v) While passing orders or making suggestions, all officers are to confine their note to the actual points he/she proposes to make. If the officer agrees to the line of action suggested in the preceding note, they can append their signature/or endorse their approval. Officer deciding to differ from the one suggested on file, he/she may do so with reasons for such a decision. (vi) Any noting on a file in which a running summary of facts is readily available, attention to the facts of the case must be drawn with reference to the appropriate part of the summary, without having to repeat it in Officers note. (vii) Extracts of the provisions of the Act, Rules and/or guidelines will be placed in the file, with attention drawn to them in the Note, unless reiteration of such extracts are very essential in the note for facilitating decision making by the competent authority. (viii) When a summary of facts is available in the file or in the last note on the file, which could serve the expected purpose of decision making, only a self-contained note must be put up with every case submitted to the Secretary General. Such a self-contained note, will however, bring out in brief and in clear terms the relevant facts, including views expressed on the subject by other Department (s) if any, consulted in the matter, and the particular point or sequential points on which the order or decision of the Secretary General is being solicited. (ix) Self-contained notes must be prepared in seeking advice/opinion or concurrence of another Branch/Division, and such references are to be made with the approval of the Joint Secretary or higher Officer specified. (x) When Receipts for submission raises several major points requiring detailed examination for respective orders, each point (or group of related points) must be noted upon separately in sectional notes in a manner beginning with a list of major point(s) dealt with therein, placed below the main note. (xi) Only if apparent errors or incorrect statements in a file under submission have to be pointed out, or if considered views/ opinions have to be expressed therein, or to be countered, the same must be made or observed in through a courteous/temperate language avoiding any personal remarks. (xii) All Notes must contain serially numbered paragraphs in its body, with brief titles if required, for problem solving or policy decisions. 11 (xiii) While preparing physical notes, care must be taken to spread over both sides of a note sheet, provision for small margin on all sides (left, right, top and bottom) of each page of the note sheet to ensure better preservation. Scope of noting by Branch 3.11 When line of action on any receipt for submission is understandable, or is based on clear precedent/ practice, or has been directed by the Branch Officer/Divisional Officer for submission of the receipt, the file must be submitted for approval with ‘to the point’ sufficient noting only. For other receipts, the Branch will submit a detailed note. 3.12 It will be the duty of the Branch: (a) to see whether all the facts pertaining to the Receipt, conducive to them, are correctly assimilated in the Note for submission; (b) to identify and point out any mistakes or mis-statements of facts as mentioned in the receipt; (c) to draw attention to statutory or customary Procedures, Law/Rules governing the subject, by mentioning them and stating their location for perusal; (d) to place on record through the Note for submission, other relevant facts and figures available with the Secretariat, along with precedents or papers containing previous decisions of policy etc.; (e) to ponder over specific question or questions for consideration by the authorities, and to reflect the points entailing decisions by such an authority; and (f) to propose a route/path of action for the required decision making by the authority. 3.13 The following instructions shall be observed by Branches/Units/Offices for Noting on receipts received by them: (a) Any noting must be written in plain/simple and understandable English/Hindi language. Inappropriate/Lopsided lengthy noting must be consciously avoided, as only a summary of proposal on the subject may require attention of the authority. (b) Any noting must be officially moderate/pleasant in presentation, free from individual remarks. Incongruent errors or if the opinion expressed by other Department has to be pointed out for disapproval in the note, such observations must be reflected in polite/considerate words. All such notings must be expressed in third person only. (c) In case of a running file, the current ‘receipt under deliberation’ in continuity of the previous notes, if any, must be pointed out to the officer to whom the file is submitted. Reproduction of verbatim extracts from the all preceding receipts or official communications from other Department(s) must be avoided. (d) In case of lengthy/complex receipt(s), a précis must be made for submission. However, such a précis of the contents or the history of the file must not be ordinarily prepared, until instructed to do. (e) A separate statement or appendix reflecting appropriate information, whose inclusion in the noting might obscure the main point(s) on issue or may make the note for submission lengthy, must be placed on the file as additional appendix for perusal of the authority. (f) When dealing with several points or orders of the current receipt under examination, each point should be reflected separately in the note of the Branch, instead of a continuous note, facilitating the Branch Officer/or higher Officers for recording their orders separately on each point of ‘Branch Note’ which could be amalgamated to form the note on the file for purposes of issue of orders, etc. (g) Note on any receipt submitted by the Branch must be done so, only after adequate discussion by the dealing hand and the Head of the Branch, so that the proposal in the note only summarises the 12 position on the subject of the receipt for precise decision making (including the alternate suggestion on any point for decision making). (h) The noting must follow sequencing in serial number for flow of correspondence, without any interruption in the continuity of the note. Submission of any receipt independent of the main file must be amalgamated with the main file at the earliest. (i) Excluding routine matters, no note should be written on the receipt itself. Remarks/direction of any Officer made on the Receipt must be mentioned in the notes before the deliberation of the Branch. (j) In case of physical file submission, space must be kept for noting/signatures by higher officers. Notes to be submitted to Branch Officer or higher Officers must not finish at the bottom of a page. Additional blank sheet must be placed as a courtesy sheet to the notes. (k) All notices/requests received from Members of Parliament or Officers on paper/slips (of small size) must be pasted on to a foolscap size white sheet before taking them on a file for submission by the Branch on usual lines of submission. (l) Long noting in the margin on any physical file must be avoided, or must be removed before submitting the file to hierarchy of Officers. (m) While replying to a letter on mandated lines, only a ‘draft for approval’ with a note mentioning ‘draft reply submitted for approval’ must be submitted with reproducing any substance of the reply in the notes. (n) Submission note for all the Letters, Files or other communications received from other Departments, Ministries or Offices or Persons, must be done on a separate note sheet, rather than submitting the Secretariat’s note on any additional sheet/sheets contained in such communications received. That is, all Inter-departmental correspondence between this Secretariat and other Ministries or Departments must be kept separately without mixing them with the internal notings. (o) The Official presenting the approval note on a receipt must append his/her initials and date on the left hand side below his/her note. The Head of the Branch will put his/her dated initials below the note submitted, for either disposing the receipt within his/her delegated powers or for forwarding the submission to an Officer in the hierarchy. The competent authority may sign on the right hand side of notes. (p) In a physical file all markings to higher Officers should be in the margin of the note. (q) Notes for submission, soliciting order of HS/HDS and SG, must be concise, self-contained and must be submitted by the Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) through the concerned Joint Secretary/Additional Secretary/Secretary. Also, notes concerning more than one Branch seeking orders of HS/HDS and SG must be submitted in a consolidated manner by the Divisional Officer, specifically mentioning the points requiring approval. Upon approval of the highest authority, Officers in the down chain must not append their initials on the right hand side of the note sheet. Any or all marking/initials must be in the margin of the note sheet only. (r) If further note is required to be put up, it should be on the new note sheet bearing the name of the Branch or Office of the officer who has initiated that note and not in continuation of the note on which HS/HDS/SG has passed orders. Action by Head of the Branch 3.14 Head of the Branch will study/examine the noting under submission by the dealing hand and may dispose such items of work without reference to his/her Branch/Divisional Officer: (i) Grant of casual leave/compensatory leave/special leave up to three days; (ii) Issue of reminders and acknowledgements; (iii) Recording of files; 13 (iv) Issue of Office Orders, Routine Orders and Circulars of ephemeral natures; (v) Any other case, which by a general or specific office order, Head of Branch is authorised to dispose of independently. 3.15 The delegations under (v) above have been made vide OO Part-I Nos.316 and 359 dated 18th February, 1957 and 25th October, 1957 respectively. 3.16 While signing official communications relating to matter within officer’s own power, the Head of Branch may use his/her name and designation. Authentication of Orders 3.17 Although, the powers delegated to Head of Branch for disposal of certain cases and issuing of communications over their signatures, all orders passed by or made in the name of the Speaker, shall be authenticated by the signature of an officer not below the rank of Under Secretary. Noting by Branch Officer 3.18 A Branch Officer must resolve all the receipts falling under his/her delegated administrative/financial powers on his/her own responsibility. Orders of the Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) or higher Officers must be obtained on files pertaining to important nature or those involving question of policy. The officer must make an effort to reduce the number of receipts to be submitted to the Divisional Officer by seeking his/her verbal directions. 3.19 While submitting files for the consideration of higher officers, with suggestions/ recommendations, the officer/official/individual must confine his/her note to the points of issue that needs to be dealt by him/her. When the officer concurs with the suggestions/recommendations made in the note made by the Branch, the officer append his/her signature or indicate his/her approval for the proposal. 3.20 Proposals, wherein a note under submission has been approved by an officer of a particular Branch are sent to an officer of another Branch or any Branch for comments or examination of the proposal or for similar purpose, the officer, to whom the file is marked, should invariably present the reply note himself/ herself. Such an officer may ask his/her Branch to examine the matter or furnish factual information for the purpose of the officer’s own reflection. The Branch, in such a case, should submit a separate note for the information of the Branch Officer, who shall ultimately record his/her note on the file. Branch must not make noting on files approved at the Officer level. 3.21 In e-File, sending/marking of receipts/files are flexible. The system allows a user to send a receipt/ file to any other user and the movement of record is maintained (who has sent, to whom has been sent and when has been sent). Physical files which is marked to another officer has to be received by him/her by clicking appropriate button in his/her inbox indicating that the physical file has been received at his/her end. The acknowledgement for the same should be obtained from the recipient. Electronic file once marked to the next user goes to his/her inbox indicating that it has been received by him/her. Notes and orders by Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) 3.22 The Divisional Officer should endeavor to settle all appropriate receipts channeled to him/her on his/her own responsibility under the delegated powers. The Divisional Officer may use his/her discretion in taking orders of the Joint Secretary/Additional Secretary/Secretary or Secretary-General on all important receipts requiring approval at an appropriate level of competence. Oral instruction obtained after direct discussion with any higher authority must be recorded as far as possible. Self-contained note for HS/HDS/Chairperson of Parliamentary Committee 3.23 Whenever orders of HS/HDS/Chairperson of Parliamentary Committee/Convener of Sub-Committee of a Parliamentary Committee are to be solicited on any matter, a self-contained note shall be submitted. The 14 following instructions shall be observed in the preparation and submission of such self-contained notes: (a) The note will be given a heading as follows:— __________Branch Subject...................... (b) The contents of the note should be concise and to the point and will be divided into paragraphs, each dealing with a particular aspect of the subject and each paragraph duly numbered. (c) The note shall contain a concise background of the case and the orders relevant to the subject matter and reference to the statutory or customary procedure or previous decisions or precedents, if any. If the case is based on the provisions of any rules, regulations, statute or past precedents, action to be taken will also be suggested. (d) If the inclusion of any information in the note is likely to obscure the main point at issue or makes the note unnecessarily lengthy, a separate statement or appendix giving the information will be placed on the file. (e) The last paragraph of the note should invariably state precisely the question or questions for consideration or point on which the orders are solicited. (f) The note should be neatly typed/written on both sides of the paper/note-sheet in single-spacing with a quarter margin on green note-sheet and should not contain unnecessary erasures, omissions or additions. (g) The self-contained note to the HS/HDS/Chairperson/Convener should in the first instance be signed by the Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) and submitted through Joint Secretary, Additional Secretary, Secretary and Secretary-General. (h) The self-contained note, together with the relevant papers that are to be put up with it to the HS/ HDS/Chairperson/Convener will be submitted in a separate file cover which will bear the number and subject of the main file. After the Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) has approved it, he/she will return the main file to the Branch and submit the self-contained note to the Secretary-General through the Joint Secretary/Additional Secretary/Secretary. (i) If the Divisional Officer (Director or Officer holding equivalent rank) wants to put up a note in connection with the self-contained note for the information of Joint Secretary/Additional Secretary/ Secretary/Secretary-General, he/she will do so on a separate note sheet which will be returned to him/her and the self-contained note forwarded to the HS/HDS/Chairperson/Convenor by the Personal Staff of Secretary-General, Secretary, Additional Secretary or Joint Secretary as the case may be. (j) When the note is received back from HS/HDS/Chairperson/Convenor with his/her orders thereon, all markings/initials should be done in the margin of the note sheet. No further noting will be done on the sheet or sheets containing the orders. All further noting will be done on a fresh and separate note sheet so that the self-contained note and HS/HDS/Chairperson/Convenor’s orders thereon remain in the file in a separate file cover as a self-contained documents which can be utilised for further reference, if necessary. (k) If any further information is to be submitted to HS/HDS/Chairperson/Convenor on the same matter or his/her orders thereon are to be taken again, further noting will be done on a separate note sheet in continuation of the previous self-contained note and it will not be necessary to summarise the position in a fresh self-contained note every time the file is submitted to HS/HDS/Chairperson Convener. (l) Highlighters should not be used for highlighting of notes. 3.24 When a file has to be sent to the Hon’ble Speaker, the following instructions must be observed:– (a) Such a file should contain only information which is essential to facilitate the Hon’ble Speaker to 15 arrive at a decision without calling for additional facts or references. All papers which are irrelevant to the point at issue should be removed before submission. (b) Essential references contained in the filed papers should be extracted, placed in the file and referenced. (c) All papers placed in the file should be legible. Communications (including fax/e-mail message received from Ministries/Departments, etc.) must be retyped for submission if found unreadable. 2. Drafting Draft—When to be prepared 3.25 Except when the line of action on a case is obvious, and orders have been obtained from the competent officer indicating the terms of the reply to be sent, a draft of the communication proposed to be sent out must be prepared for approval of such officer, and upon approval of the draft, a fair letter may be submitted for his/ her signature(s). A Branch Officer or a higher Officer who has formulated his/her ideas on a case may himself/ herself prepare a draft and authorise its issue or submit it to the next higher officer for approval, as the case may be. In all other cases, the draft will be prepared by the Branch. 3.26 The following general instructions must be followed as regards drafting: (a) A draft should be typed in double space, with half margin and on both sides of the paper. (b) The Letter No. and date of the communication replied to or of the last communication in a series of correspondence on the same subject should be referred to or invited. Where it is necessary to refer to more than one communication or a series of communications, this should be done in the margin of the draft. The subject should be mentioned invariably in all communications including reminders. (c) The draft should indicate the enclosures which are to accompany the fair copy. To draw the attention of the typist, the comparers and the dispatcher, a diagonal stroke should be made in the margin. The number of enclosures also be indicated at the end of the draft on the left bottom of the page ‘Encls. Nos.’ (d) If copies of an enclosure referred to in the draft are available and have not therefore to be typed, the fact should be clearly stated in the margin of the draft for the guidance of the typist. (e) All drafts put up on a file should bear the registered number of the file. When two or more letters, notifications, etc. are to be issued from the same file on the same date to the same addressee the serial number should also be given in addition in order to avoid confusion in reference, thus (i) 8/5(I)/2009-O&M and (ii) 8/5(II)/2009-O&M. (f) Where State Governments or Ministries, etc., are consulted on any matter, time limit for replies should ordinarily be specified. The officer in whose signature the communication is to be issued to will initial on the draft in token of his/her approval. His/her designation should invariably be indicated on the draft. (g) Text of any type of communication, including e-mail, to be sent to any Department/Office within or outside Lok Sabha Secretariat shall be approved by the Divisional Officer concerned. (h) A flag bearing the words ‘Draft for Approval’ should be attached to the draft. When more than one draft is submitted at the same time, they should be numbered I, II, III and so on. Collection of Model Drafts (i) In order to ensure that drafts which are prepared after great thought and careful examination are not lost in files and thus become unavailable at the time when they are required for the disposal of similar references later on, copies of all model drafts should be collected in a separate file. (j) For quick reference, an index to the collection of model drafts must be maintained by each Branch. The subjects of the index will be arranged in alphabetical order, devoting each page to a letter or letters as the case may be. 16 (k) In the course of day to day disposal of cases, as and when important communications are drafted, the Head of the Branch must have spare copies of such drafts for adding them to the collection, indexing them under appropriate subjects. (l) The collection of model drafts must be scrutinized in the beginning of every year and the obsolete drafts found must be weeded out. Drafts which are subsequently improved must replace the last old drafts on the subject. Style (m) A draft should convey the exact intention of the order passed. The language used should be clear, concise and incapable of misconstruction. Lengthy sentences, abruptness, redundancy, circumlocution, superlative and repetition (whether of words, expressions or ideas) should be avoided. Communication of some length or complexity should generally be concluded with a summary. (n) The following general principles may be followed by all concerned: (i) Words that are necessary to express one’s meaning should be used, so that the correct meaning to be conveyed is not obscured. (ii) Extra adjectives, adverbs, and roundabout phrases must be avoided. (iii) Readily understandable and familiar words must be preferred against the use of farfetched words. (iv) Words expressing precise meaning should be preferred to the words those that are vague, so that the thoughts conveyed clearly. (v) Concrete words should be preferred to abstract words for they are more likely to have precise meaning. (o) The use of participles is sometimes very convenient in the drafts. The following list will meet most of the cases:– Acknowledging Communicating Notifying Admitting Directing Proclaiming Advising Enclosing Recommending Appealing Enquiring Reporting Appointing Explaining Requesting Affirming Forwarding Sanctioning Authorising Intimating Stating Cancelling Inviting Submitting Confirming Nominating (p) Vague words and phrases that have crept into the official style and claim the sanction of tradition include ‘therein, thereon, thereof, in respect of, in regard to, as regards, in relation to, for being, do the needful, for necessary action or necessary instructions, respectively, etc .’ Words such as these tend to obscure the meaning. For the words ‘therein, thereon and thereof ’ the simple words ‘in it, on it, or of it’ would have served the purpose. Likewise, ‘in relation to’ displaces in many cases the word ‘towards’. Anxiety to avoid repetition leads to the use of ‘former’ and ‘latter’, but this places undue strain on the reader’s memory. Such vague expressions should be avoided. (q) A phrase which has been much overworked in official communications is ‘as to’. It often appears unnecessarily along with the words ‘whether, who, what etc.’ For example, in the sentence “The 17 Administrative Officer is requested to report as to whether the case has been completed”, ‘as to’ is redundant and should be omitted. (r) Some of the errors which are common to official writing are given below and care should be taken to avoid these mistakes: (i) The words ‘Government’, ‘Secretariat’, ‘Branch’, ‘Committee’ are sometimes used in singular and sometimes in plural. The correct procedure is to use them in the plural form, but if the singular is used, it should be constantly followed throughout the sentence and should not be changed as has been done in the following sentence: “The Secretariat has considered your case carefully but have come to the conclusion.” Likewise, the mood also gets mixed up frequently. An example of change in mood is given below: “When I referred the matter to the Committee, it was considered by me.” The correct form should be: “ When I referred the matter to the Committee, I considered.” It is equally important to see that tense used throughout is the same. (ii) After ‘suggest’ use ‘should’ not ‘may’ (after ‘request’ use ‘may’ not ‘should’). (iii) ‘Point out’ is a much abused phrase. It should really be used in speaking of some fact or a circumstance of which the addressee ought to have been aware from the source of information open to him/her. It should never be used as synonymous with ‘explain’ or ‘inform you’. (iv) ‘However’ is a word which often gets misplaced. To illustrate, lets examine a sentence “after careful consideration (1) of these suggestions, (2) the Government of India are unable (3) to agree that”. In this sentence, (2) is the right place for ‘however’ and not (1) or (3). It should come between commas, fairly near but not too near the beginning. (v) Wrong use of the words ‘had’ and ‘have’ is also frequent. The past perfect ‘had’ is to be used only to emphasise the priority of one event in the past over another e.g., it is correct to say “I had gone to Shimla when the Chairman left the place”. But it is a wrong usage in the sentence “I had gone to Shimla last Friday”. (vi) Many words are used without a proper implication of their meaning. When the Officer asks for a file and the file is lost, the dealing hand often puts up a note saying that it is ‘not available’. To say that the file is not available does not mean that it is lost. It only means that the file has been kept somewhere else or sent to some other office. The use of the words ‘in case’, for the word’ if ‘ and the phrase ‘as well as’ an equivalent of ‘and’ are other instances. When the dealing hand writes, “the file will be put up in case the Member does not pay the rent on the due date”, he/she means that “the file will be put up if the Member does not pay the rent on the due date”. (vii) The words ‘till’ and’ all’ also come in for a good deal of mishandling. When a dealing hand puts up a file to the Officer stating that no return was received till the 1st of December, it actually means that a return was received on the 1st December. But this is not what the dealing hand wants to say. What the dealing hand has in mind is that no return was received even on the 1st of December. To convey that, the word ‘upto’ followed by the word ‘had’ would have been correct e.g., “up to December 1st the return had not been received”. Similarly, when a dealing hand reports that “all the Junior Clerks have not passed the Senior Clerk Test”, what he/she means is that “not a single clerk has passed the Senior Clerk Test”. But what he/she actually conveys is that there are some Junior Clerks who have passed the Senior Clerk Test. 18 (viii) Omission of the article and use of the wrong preposition are also frequently met with. The following are some of the examples of wrong usage:— Incorrect Correct In Compliance of — In compliance with In the margin — On the margin In this behalf — On his/her behalf To kindly see — To see kindly Dispose it off — Dispose it of Under the circumstances — In the circumstances To thoroughly investigate — To investigate thoroughly Comprising of — Comprising The following words are often wrongly used:— Acquaint for Inform or tell. Advert for Refer. Adumbrate for Sketch, outline, foreshadow. Ameliorate for Better, . Assist for Help. Blue-print for Plan. Ceiling for Limit. Cross-section for Sample. Commence for Begin. Deem for Think. Conditioned by for Dependent on. Consider for Think. Drive(intr.) for Came, originate, spring. Develop for Take place, occur, happen, grow. Entail for Impose, necessitate. Envisage for Contemplate, face. Eventuate for Come about, happen, occur, result, turnout. Evince for Show, manifest, display. Factor for Fact, consideration, circumstances, feature, element, constituent. Function (verb) for Work, operate, act. Inform for Tell. In isolation for By itself. Initiate for Begin, start. Locality for Place. Major for Important, chief, main, principal. Majority, The. for Most. Materialise for Come about, happen, occur. Minimise for Under-estimate, disparage, belittle, make light of. Practically for Virtually, almost, nearly, all but. 19 Proceed for Go. A percentage of for Some. A Proportion of for Some. Purchase for Buy. Reaction for Opinion, view. Render for Make. Reside for Live. Residence for Home. State for Say. Stress(verb) for Emphasise. Sufficient for Enough. Terminate for End. Transmit for Send, forward. Visualise for Imagine, picture.
